title: Ravana lifts the mountain
hookLine: Ravana tries to lift Shiva's mountain and ends up singing under it; why a temple's peak is for bowing
carry: the ego lifts; the devotee bows

cards: Ravana is flying home in the Pushpaka, the flying chariot he has just taken from his own half-brother, and he has never been more sure of himself. Then, over a mountain in the far north, the chariot stops dead.
It won't go on. Shiva's attendant Nandi steps out. This is Kailash, he says.
Shiva and Parvati are here. Go around. Ravana laughs.
Go around? He climbs down, gets his twenty arms under the mountain, and lifts.

teach.h: ONE TOE, AND THE MOUNTAIN SETTLES.
teach.b: The mountain shakes. Parvati catches hold of Shiva. And Shiva, without even getting up, presses down with one toe.
The mountain settles, and Ravana's arms are pinned beneath it. He roars with pain so loud the worlds tremble. His ministers tell him there's only one way out: praise the one you tried to move.
So, pinned under the mountain, he sings to Shiva, and the old telling says he sang for a thousand years.
At last Shiva lets him go and gives him a name: Ravana, the one who roared.

At Ellora, in western India, a whole temple is cut down into one cliff of rock and named for Kailash itself, and on its side Ravana shakes the mountain while Shiva calmly holds it still with his foot.

That's the shikhara idea: a temple's tower is often said to echo a holy mountain, Kailash or Meru. You don't climb it and stand on top. You come in under it, to the small dark room at its heart, and you bow.

Hindus have a name for the part of you that tries to lift the mountain, and many teachers read Ravana here as just that: ahamkara, the I-maker, the ego that says mine, I did it. Ravana was strong enough to shake Kailash.
Strength just wasn't the way in. Bowing was.
Today is the top of year one: words, stories, practices, a whole scripture read through, the depths.
The ahamkara would love to stand up here and say, done, I've got this. The tradition's move is the other one. At the top, you bow.

how: Many Hindus bow on entering a temple, before the shrine and before elders, and touch an elder's feet for a blessing; the Kailasa temple at Ellora, cut from a single rock, carries a well-known carving of Ravana shaking Kailash.

o: the final goal, where the journey is over
a base camp where climbers rest overnight
a mountain peak, a summit to look back from

games.q: who's who under the mountain — tap the pairs.
p: a temple tower echoing a mountain

s: Shiva fought Ravana with weapons to save Kailash
he didn't even get up. one toe pressed down, and the mountain settled.
Ravana's name comes from his roar under the mountain
pinned under Kailash, he cried out so loud the worlds shook, and Shiva named him for it.
a temple's shikhara is built for people to climb and stand on
it echoes a holy mountain. you come in under it, to the shrine at its heart, and bow.

games.q: you've climbed for a whole year and reached the top. what does the Kailash story say to do there?
o: stand on the peak and say i've got this now.
bow: the ego can't lift the mountain.
find a bigger mountain to lift.
games.why: Ravana was strong enough to shake Kailash, and it pinned him. singing to Shiva set him free. at the top, the move is to bow.

practice: Let the year come back in a few pictures: a word, a story, a flame. Notice the small voice that wants to say I did that.

Then do what Hindus do on entering a temple or meeting an elder: bow, in your body if you can, or in your mind. If you pray, offer the whole year back to God. If you don't, simply let it be bigger than you, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Shikhara, a mountain peak, and the name for the tower over a north Indian temple's shrine, often said to echo the holy mountain. You don't stand on it. You come in under it, and bow.

orig.note: Sanskrit śikhara: a mountain peak, and also the name for the tall tower over a north Indian temple's shrine.

carryVoice: Your line: the ego lifts; the devotee bows. Ravana learned it under Kailash. Day three hundred thirty.
